title: Understanding a Forage Analysis Report — Precision Feed Manager (Cornell Cooperative Extension, Delaware County)
provenance_note: Faithfully indexed from the original two-page illustrated PDF. These are source-specific forage quality goals and interpretation tips, not universally validated acceptance criteria for every crop, silo or farm. The sample report screenshot is illustrative, not a database of Wonder Milk or CVAS assay results. Original PDF binary/link is not stored in this code index.

pages.title: Forage report interpretation: DM, crude and soluble protein, ash, minerals, lignin and fiber
pages.text:
Document heading: Precision Feed Manager — Understanding a Forage Analysis Report. Cornell University Cooperative Extension of Delaware County.
How to read columns: Forages are evaluated on a dry matter (DM) basis. Most forage nutrient values should be evaluated in the DM column; percent dry matter itself is listed in the As Fed column.
Dry Matter (DM) goals based on storage type: silage bunks/piles 33–35%; silage towers/bags 33–38%; baleage 38–50%. These are goals from this guide rather than universal thresholds.
Crude Protein (CP): The document describes CP as less important than NDF for forage evaluation. Targets: hay crops 15–20%; corn silage 7–9%. Corn silage CP above 9% can indicate immaturity at harvest when accompanied by high NDF and low starch.
Soluble protein: Silages (especially hay crops) goal less than 55% of CP. Wet silages can have higher soluble protein.
Ash: Haycrop target less than 9%; corn silage less than 5%. Above these values often suggests soil contamination.
Minerals: Potassium above 2.50% in haycrops is a concern and may indicate excess potash fertilization. Iron above 300 ppm raises concern about soil or metal contamination. Guide recommends wet chemistry methods for the most accurate mineral analysis.
NDICP and ADICP = Neutral Detergent Insoluble Crude Protein and Acid Detergent Insoluble Crude Protein. These represent CP bound to NDF and ADF and are used to predict rumen protein availability.
NDF = Neutral Detergent Fiber. Higher NDF relates to gut fill and can limit forage intake. Earlier cutting of hay generally produces lower NDF. Forms mentioned: aNDF and aNDFom (organic matter basis). NDF intake can be expressed relative to animal bodyweight.
uNDFom = undigested NDF at a stated time point of rumen-fluid incubation; estimates the fiber fraction not digested.
NDFD = NDF digestibility, evaluated at several incubation times in rumen fluid; compare the same forage type at the same incubation time. The guide says 30 hours is commonly used. May also be reported as aNDFDom.
NDF goals: grass hay and silage 48–55%; MMG hay/silage 40–50%; MML hay/silage 38–45%; legume hay/silage 36–42%; corn silage 38–44%. Corn silage NDF above 44% may suggest harvest immaturity. MMG and MML abbreviations appear as written; the source does not expand them.
Lignin: Indigestible portion of fiber that generally increases with plant maturity. Cutting date and interval influence haycrop lignin; BMR hybrid selection is mentioned for corn. The guide states heat increases lignin content and first-cut haycrop is usually more digestible than second cutting.
Key message printed on page: 'Get the NDF and DM right and a lot of the rest will follow.'

pages.title: Forage report interpretation: NFC, starch and digestibility, NEL, sugars and silage fermentation
pages.text:
Document heading: Precision Feed Manager — Understanding a Forage Analysis Report. Page 2 continues the illustrated example analysis report.
Reading columns: Forage nutrients are evaluated on a dry matter (DM) basis. % dry matter is in the As Fed column; other forage concentrations discussed in the guide are generally evaluated on the DM column.
Repeated Dry Matter goals by storage: silage bunks/piles 33–35%; silage towers/bags 33–38%; baleage 38–50%.
NFC = Non Fiber Carbohydrates: measure or estimate of starch, sugar and pectin. NFC was relied upon more when laboratories did not routinely measure starch and sugar directly.
Corn silage starch goal greater than 30% DM; may reach approximately 40% in conventionally harvested (not high chop) corn. High measured starch is not necessarily adequate available starch when silage is too dry and intact corn kernels pass through the cow undigested. Haycrop forage contains comparatively little starch.
Starch digestibility: the guide describes an estimate of ruminal digestibility at 7 hours. High >88%; Moderate 79–87%; Low <78%. Do not invent classification for the unmentioned boundary values.
NEL (Net Energy of Lactation), Mcal/lb, is an estimated/calculated energy concentration. Haycrop target >0.65 Mcal/lb and corn silage target >0.70 Mcal/lb. The guide says quality NDF content/digestibility, corn silage starch, adequate DM and good fermentation contribute to energy quality.
WSC = Water Soluble Carbohydrates. ESC = Ethanol Soluble Carbohydrates. Both measure plant sugars; use ESC for evaluating silage fermentation per this guide.
High-quality silages often have sugar concentrations 3–8%. Silage sugars below 3% can reflect low sugar at harvest (e.g. long time in windrow) or extended fermentation in the silo. Very dry silage, baleage or hay may contain over 10% sugars because little fermentation consumed them.
Silage fermentation goals in this guide: lactic acid >3% of DM; acetic acid <3% of DM; VFA score >7.0.
These values are the document's general reference goals. They are not measured results for a particular Wonder Milk or CVAS sample; an actual lab report is needed for sample-specific grading.
